schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch make the untitled psalm the continuation of the Psalm 9 acrostic — begins with lamed, drops mem to tsade, resumes at the close, so the two psalms compose one broken alphabet; note it and Psalm 33 are the only anonymous psalms in Book I.
Augustine hears the delay as mercy — God 'despises in due seasons, in tribulations,' inflaming men's longing for his coming, since the fountain of life is sweeter to the thirsty.

Gill: God is never far by essence, so 'afar off' means the withdrawing of his gracious presence and deferring of help; Calvin: the words are spoken by anthropathy, the psalm a mirror of a corrupt society held up lest the faithful despair.

Henry: 'we stand afar off from God by our unbelief, and then complain that God stands afar off from us'; Spurgeon: not the trouble but the hiding of the Father's face cuts to the quick — the refiner is never far from the furnace (1 Pet. 1:6).
Clarke adds the historical setting, referring the psalm to the days of the captivity and its enemies who beheld the oppression and seemed to disregard it.

debates.question: Is this an independent psalm or the continuation of the Psalm 9 acrostic?

sides.position: one alphabet with Psalm 9 — the acrostic broken across the two, the Septuagint and Vulgate uniting them
a distinct, anonymous psalm as the received Hebrew and English divide it

outliers.note: Reads the delay allegorically as a design of mercy — God withdraws seasonably to inflame the thirst of the little ones for his coming, so that even the permitting of evil serves to make the truth the sweeter.

schools.summary: Henry divides the charge into pride and persecution, the former the cause of the latter, tyranny owing its origin to pride; Spurgeon reads a formal indictment and a just petition — 'we weigh you in your own scales,' Haman on his own gallows.
Gill fixes the 'poor' as the gracious man, poor in goods and in spirit, and the verb as hot pursuit, antichrist hunting the followers of the Lamb.
Clarke: no natural principle accounts for the hatred — the wicked persecutes godliness only because 'the devil is in his heart.'

Ellicott, with LXX/Aquila/Symmachus/Vulgate, makes the sufferer the subject — 'in the pride of the wicked the sufferer burns,' the plural then displacing the singular; Keil and Delitzsch keep the persecutor, the perfect tenses recording a settled, self-praising character.

debates.question: Who is the subject of the opening line — the persecutor or the sufferer?

sides.position: 'the wicked in his pride doth persecute the poor' (the persecutor acts)
'in the pride of the wicked the sufferer burns' (the poor is the subject, of his affliction), with LXX/Aquila/Symmachus/Vulgate

schools.summary: Spurgeon's boaster thrice condemned — silly, brazen, abandoned; Henry sets the boast against heaven's verdict, God and men differing in their sentiments, the friendship of the world enmity with God.
Clarke: to boast of iniquity is the broad road to perdition; Wesley: he glories in his very sins, which are his shame.
Gill renders with the Chaldee and Jarchi, 'the wicked praiseth himself for the desire of his heart.'

Ellicott: literally 'speaketh praise to the lust of his soul' (the villain addressing his own passions); 'blesseth' is 'rather curseth by a common euphemism' (Job 1:5), 'the covetous' (robber) subject or object — 'the robber curseth, despiseth Jehovah.'

debates.question: Does the second clause read 'blesseth the covetous' or 'curseth (and despiseth) the LORD'?

sides.position: 'blesseth the covetous, whom the LORD abhorreth' — the received reading
'curseth (and) despiseth Jehovah' — 'bless' as the common euphemism for 'curse,' with the ancient versions

schools.summary: Gill supplies 'after God' (Targum, Kimchi) — the wicked will not seek to God, pray, or inquire into his will, all from a pride shown in the haughty countenance 'more stout than his fellows.'
Clarke: too proud to bend his knee or put on sackcloth, and so certain to perish; Wesley: pride, though seated in the heart, is named of the countenance because there most manifest.
Henry makes the verse a definition of irreligion — not seeking after God nor having him in our thoughts (Job 35:10) — whose cause is pride, men thinking their own hands sufficient.
Ellicott says the AV 'has quite missed the meaning': 'the wicked in his haughtiness (height of his nostril) saith, He will not requite it; there is no God in all his thought' (Ps. 14:1; 53:1).

debates.question: How should the verse be rendered?

sides.position: 'will not seek after God; God is not in all his thoughts' — the proud man's practical godlessness
'in his haughtiness he saith, He will not requite it; there is no God in all his thought' — the fool's positive denial

schools.summary: Gill lays out the renderings of 'his ways are always grievous' — cause terror (Aben Ezra), are defiled (LXX/Vulg), always remain, or prosper (Jarchi), the last stumbling the saints.

Ellicott: better 'his enterprises always succeed' or 'his ways are always strong' (Job 20:21); 'a height, thy judgments, far above him' (Ps. 36:6); 'puffeth' in scorn, quoting South on puffing at damnation.

Clarke: 'he is travailing in pain to bring forth iniquity at all times,' blind to God's hand, whistling at his foes like an Eastern despot; Wesley: the puffing a gesture of contempt, sure he can blow his enemies away.
Henry: he turns off every warning — never saw God, counts his judgments mere bugbears, far above out of his sight.

debates.question: What does 'his ways are always grievous' mean?

sides.position: grievous / defiled / cause terror / prosper — a spread of received renderings
'his enterprises always succeed' or 'his ways are always strong' — the tyrant's bold, prospering course
'he is travailing in pain to bring forth iniquity' — a labour of sin

themes: judgments far above out of sight

schools.summary: Gill notes it is said 'in his heart,' the thought being the speech of the mind — a settled inward persuasion.
Clarke grounds the confidence in possessions — 'I have whatever I covet, money and goods to procure every gratification.'

Keil and Delitzsch hear a blasphemous parody of faith — what the believer says by fellowship (Ps. 16:8) the wicked says in godless self-confidence, looking to an endless future without evil; Ellicott: 'I shall never be moved at any time: I who am without ill.'
Henry sets the boast among doomed securities — like Babylon, 'I shall be a lady for ever' (Isa. 47:7; Rev. 18:7): 'those are nearest ruin who thus set it furthest from them.'

themes: the parody of the saint's assurance

schools.summary: Gill: 'he has filled his mouth with cursing' — an oath, whether profane or false and defrauding, in the man of sin the mouth speaking blasphemies.
Ellicott: cursing joined with deceit (Hos. 4:2) means perjury; Keil and Delitzsch begin the figure of the lier in wait, against a background of anarchy like Hosea's (Hos. 6:9).
Clarke: 'a blasphemer, a deceitful man, and a knave!'; Wesley: under fair speeches mischief is hid, and 'vanity' is better read as injury and oppression.
Henry: 'where there is a heart full of malice there is commonly a mouth full of curses' — venom spat at those he cannot harm, hatred covered with deceit (Prov. 26:26).
Gill: the word may mean 'palaces' or 'courts' (Chaldee/Syriac), the LXX's 'lurking places with the rich' — persons of note, antichrist in the temple, his emissaries in the congregations.
Clarke reads espionage and the private murderer's craft, eyes privily set; Wesley places him in the ways bordering the villages, as robbers use, 'privily set' being literally 'hid.'

Ellicott: 'villages' properly enclosed places, even an unwalled hamlet or encampment (Gen. 25:16); 'the poor' a word peculiar to this psalm (vv.10, 14) whose root is darkness — Burgess would keep it, 'his eyes wait for the darkness' (Job 24:15).
Henry reads the ambush morally — Esau the cunning hunter, hiding not from shame or fear but lest discovery defeat his design, his malice against the innocent and poor.

debates.question: What are the 'lurking places of the villages'?

sides.position: the haunts of highwaymen among unwalled hamlets and encampments
palaces or courts — lurking 'with the rich,' persons of note

outliers.note: Follows Burgess in keeping the darkness-root of the peculiar word for 'the poor' — 'his eyes hide (wait) for the darkness,' the persecutor watching for twilight as the adulterer in Job 24:15.

themes: the peculiar word for the poor

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch trace the lion's lair (a thicket, from a root 'to interweave/cover') and note the figure reversed — the afflicted the prey, the wicked the hunter dragging him off in his net (Job 24:22); Ellicott calls it 'a confusion of metaphor,' rendering the mounting repetition 'lurks to seize a sufferer, seizes a sufferer.'
Gill reads the lion of antichrist in his civil and ecclesiastical capacity, the insidious methods that destroy the witnesses of Christ from cover.
Henry: he 'lies in wait as a lion that thirsts after blood, and feeds with pleasure upon the prey,' the devil behind him seeking 'not what, but whom, he may devour.'

themes: lieth in wait as a lion

schools.summary: Gill: the lion couching before the leap, the beast that would be thought a lamb, styling himself 'servus servorum' — the crouch the posture of the pounce.
Wesley: the lion lies close that he may not be discovered and may suddenly seize; Clarke hears the conduct of Sanballat and Tobiah (Neh. 4), the lion gathering himself 'to make the greater spring.'

Keil and Delitzsch weigh Chethib/Keri, taking Job 38:40 as the rule, the verb 'crouch down' answered by kindred Arabic; Ellicott records the rival 'is crushed' (Jerome, Syriac) making the sufferer the subject, and reads 'strong ones' as claws or strong places.

debates.question: Does the wicked 'crouch' or is the sufferer 'crushed'?

sides.position: the wicked croucheth like a beast to spring
'is crushed' — the afflicted is beaten down and sinks beneath his mighty ones

schools.summary: Gill weighs what is 'forgotten' — the wicked man's own sins (presumed impunity) or the poor he oppresses (for whom a book of remembrance is written).
Clarke hears the settled despair — God 'hath cast off this people, and will never re-establish them.'

Ellicott sharpens the tense, 'hath hidden'; Keil and Delitzsch mark this boast as the lowest point of the description and the place where, the letterless strophes ended, the acrostic gathers to resume.
Henry reads a threefold blasphemy — against God's omniscience, his holiness, and his justice — with the comfort that those abusive to God's people are abusive to God himself.

Keil and Delitzsch: 'here the acrostic arrangement is resumed with koph' — the living God called to destroy the appearance of his indifference, 'forget not' answering the ungodly's 'God hath forgotten' (Ps. 9:12).

Henry: arise to the confusion of those who say thou hidest thy face, and forget not the poor in spirit whose oppressors say God has forgotten them; Spurgeon marvels at faith's boldness mingled with unbelief — the incessant cry of the Church.
Clarke: hear their reproaches, see their guile, lift up thine hand to threaten them to repentance, and punish if they repent not.
Gill lists the ways God is contemned — his being and providence denied, his law a strange thing, his gospel foolishness, his ministers and Son disdained.
Clarke: the longsuffering of God leadeth them to repentance; Wesley turns it on the patience — 'why dost thou, by giving them impunity, suffer and occasion them to despise thee?'

Henry's double astonishment — at the wickedness (they know him not) and the patience (the reckoning not yet come); Spurgeon traces the evil to 'atheistical ideas,' and 'if there were no hell for other men, there ought to be one for those who question the justice of it.'
Keil and Delitzsch look past the taunt to its answer — the ungodly thinks God will not require it, but it is entirely otherwise, for he does see.

themes: wherefore doth the wicked contemn God

schools.summary: Gill sets the confession against the boast — though they say God will never see, he sees all, even what is thought in the heart.
Keil and Delitzsch read the deliberate answer to v.11 — God beholds mischief and spite, noting it all 'to give it into his hand,' into his own power; Ellicott dissents textually (see below).

Clarke joins seeing to requiting — nothing escapes, justice not forgotten though not speedily executed — the sufferer surrendering body, soul, and cause; Wesley reads the requital 'with thy hand' as God's own extraordinary providence.

Henry turns the oversight to comfort — God beholds all done by the hands and lurking in the hearts of oppressors, and will recompense it; Spurgeon: 'God is all-eye to see, and all-hand to punish his enemies.'

debates.question: Does the sufferer's clause read 'the poor committeth himself unto thee'?

sides.position: 'the poor committeth himself unto thee' — commits/leaves his cause to God
'the helpless leaveth it to Thee,' or by re-division 'it is against thee that he is strong in darkness'

outliers.note: By a slight change in the division and pointing of the letters floats the bolder reading 'it is against thee that he is strong in darkness,' carrying over the darkness-root of the peculiar word for the poor.

themes: to requite it with thy hand

schools.summary: Gill: 'break the arm' is to break the persecutor's power; the prayer part-fulfilled on antichrist, whose arm is broken though his kingdom stands; the accent divides the verse, 'and the evil man' going with what follows.

Keil and Delitzsch read a proverb of utter riddance — 'punish his wickedness, find nothing more of it,' evil vanished even from God's eye; Ellicott reads the same proverb (Isa. 41:12), 'thou shalt look for his wickedness and not find it' (so the LXX).
Clarke: investigate all his haunts and punish 'while there is a crime to punish,' or 'till not one transgressor is to be found'; Wesley: 'search for it, and punish these wicked atheists.'
Henry: God disables the persecutor (that the hypocrite reign not, Job 34:30) and deals with him, seeking out the wickedness he thought should lie hid and unpunished.

debates.question: What does 'seek out his wickedness till thou find none' mean?

sides.position: a proverb of riddance — God so hunts out the evil that it disappears altogether
a searching-out for punishment — investigate and punish till no transgressor remains

themes: break thou the arm of the wicked

schools.summary: Ellicott: the personal psalm 'swells out into a larger strain of national hope and faith'; Keil and Delitzsch place the poet on an eminence beholding the end, the longing of the meek for Jahve's arising now heard (Isa. 26:8).

Henry grounds it in the office of a King — to whom should the injured appeal but the sovereign, an everlasting King who judges when time shall be no more; Spurgeon reads the closing song of thanksgiving to the great and everlasting King.
Wesley and Clarke take 'the heathen perished out of his land' historically — the Canaanites whom God as King of the world expelled, all cut off or converted.
Gill reaches to the last things — Christ King over all the earth, every antichristian power destroyed, the devil, beast, and false prophet cast into the lake of fire, his kingdom everlasting.

debates.question: How far does 'the heathen are perished out of his land' reach?

sides.position: the historical Canaanites expelled from Canaan
the eschatological perishing of every enemy from the everlasting kingdom of Christ

themes: the LORD is King for ever
the heathen perished out of his land

schools.summary: Gill: the prayers here owned may lie in inward, wordless desires, all before the Lord and principally regarded, being his own preparation and the breathings of his Spirit.
Clarke's economy of grace in four steps — God prepares the heart, suggests the prayer, hears, and answers; a cry after God proceeds from a divine preparation and will surely be heard.
Keil and Delitzsch read 'thou wilt prepare their heart' of God's giving and preserving the right disposition, the 'single eye,' the steadfast heart turned wholly to him (Ps. 51:12).
Henry: God never says 'Seek in vain,' but first prepares the heart and then gives the answer of peace — 'God's working upon us is the best earnest of his working for us' (Prov. 16:1).

themes: thou hast heard the desire of the humble

schools.summary: Gill: God causes his ear to hear so as to avenge the wrongs done to the fatherless and oppressed by the man of sin.

Henry: God pleads the cause of the persecuted and ends the fury of the persecutor — 'hitherto shall they come, but no further' — for the oppressor is 'but a man of the earth,' mean and mortal (Isa. 51:12), held in a chain.

Wesley: 'to judge' is to give sentence for the oppressed against their enemies, 'the man' being mortal men who contend with their Maker; Clarke renders 'that he may not add any more to drive away the wretched man from the land,' turning it on the persecutions of his own day.

Ellicott takes 'the man of the earth' of mere mortal man over against God — 'that man of the earth may no more terrify,' or (cf. Ps. 9:20) 'that the nations may know themselves to be but men,' no longer defying Israel's God.

debates.question: Who is 'the man of the earth,' and what may he no more do?

sides.position: the tyrant/oppressor, driven from the land, that he may oppress no more
mere mortal man / the nations, that they may no more terrify or defy, knowing themselves but men (cf. Ps. 9:20)
